transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-04-20 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alex Park (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Redwood SRE), Priya Rao (Nimbus Infra), Jordan Lee (Nimbus CTO), Marco Diaz (Nimbus ML)

Summary:
Quick but deep technical session focused on recent production instability: OOMs on long-context requests, intermittent CUDA driver errors observed on their dedicated VPC deployment, request timeouts vs retries and how Redwood's runtime handles idempotency and double-execution risk. Discussed batching, KV cache behavior, quantization tradeoffs, and autoscaler interactions. Agreed to run a focused stress test and share logs + compatibility matrix.

Topics covered:
- OOM patterns and common triggers (large batch + long seq + KV cache pressure)
- Timeouts at request / transport layer and how retries are handled by Redwood agents
- CUDA errors (driver vs runtime), and kernel selection/memory pinning behaviors
- Retry semantics: idempotency, exactly-once concerns, backoff jitter, and metric impacts (cost/crediting)
- VPC/on-prem constraints: network egress, driver upgrade cadence, and HSM/KMS access for keys
- Quantization and batch sizing interaction with latency SLOs

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. we wanted to go deep into the OOMs/timeouts you saw last week and walk through the logs, right?
[00:22] Priya (Nimbus): yeah thanks Alex. we had three incidents in last 48 hours where long-context inference hit OOMs, sometimes followed by a CUDA driver termination on the node. it looks like when we hit a long tail of 10-12k token requests the node memory climbs and then boom, driver crash.
[00:45] Samir (SE): ok, good context. first quick q: are those single requests with 10k tokens or batched combos that result in similar total tokens?
[01:05] Priya: mixed. some are single huge requests from our RAG pipeline, others are retries piling up that end up being scheduled together in the runtime. We also noticed KV cache grows when we have long chat sessions, and that seems to push memory over.
[01:32] Samir: that sounds like a classic KV explosion plus batching side-effect. Our runtime keeps per-session KV cache by default and we have policies to evict stale prefixes, but if sessions are long and we pin them to a dedicated backend it can saturate GPU memory.
[01:52] Jordan (CTO): why doesn't the autoscaler bail earlier? seems like we should have had more headroom or preemptive scaling.
[02:12] Maya (SRE): the autoscaler is reactive; it's tuned for throughput not for single-request peak. If a single request allocates a huge activations tensor, autoscaler metrics (GPU util / pod CPU) don't surface soon enough to add capacity before OOM.
[02:30] Samir: right - autoscalers typically act on utilization. For single large allocations we recommend either request-level admission control (reject requests > X tokens), or a slow-path that routes very large contexts to a different pool with larger instance types or higher memory.
[02:52] Marco (ML): so the workaround is split/stream the request? we've tried partial chunking but it breaks some of our coherence requirements.
[03:10] Samir: streaming/chunking can work but needs model-aware recombination. Another lever is quantization profiles: int8 quantization may reduce activation memory, but it can change accuracy. Did you test quantized variants in this workload?
[03:32] Marco: we ran int8 on similar tasks, small quality diffs but not acceptable for some clinical prompts.
[03:45] Priya: also note that some OOMs were followed by CUDA driver resets. the node had dmesg showing nv-peer-mem and then the driver restarted. can't tell if it's a hardware error or a kernel bug.
[04:02] Samir: driver resets often indicate either exceeding GPU memory or a kernel crash in a non-recoverable path. We need the nvidia-smi --query, driver logs, and Redwood runtime logs around the timestamp. if driver dies, the process is killed and retries may re-enqueue leading to duplicate work.
[04:25] Alex: this is where retry semantics matter - we saw timeouts at the transport layer and the customer SDK retried without idempotency keys, resulting in multiple identical requests. that spiked load and worsened OOMs.
[04:45] Priya: yes. our client lib retries by default. we expected the server to dedupe. is there server dedupe?
[05:02] Samir: currently Redwood supports idempotency tokens per request - but dedupe relies on client-provided tokens and the token TTL in the control plane. For active model execution (non-fast path), dedupe is hard because if a request partially executed and then crashed during commit, we may not be able to rewind to exact snapshot. we do best-effort.
[05:28] Jordan: so what's your recommended retry/backoff policy to avoid double-charges and repeated OOM triggers?
[05:40] Samir: exponential backoff with jitter, and conservative retry count (1-2) for idempotent calls; for non-idempotent streaming generation, avoid automatic client retries. At server side, we can implement a lightweight lease: once execution starts, set a short lease so subsequent identical requests within that window are either rejected or routed to a warm fallback.
[06:05] Maya: can Redwood emit a webhook or event when execution starts so clients can be notified and not retry blindly?
[06:18] Samir: yes that's feasible; we can expose an execution-start webhook or use a short-lived transaction id returned immediately that clients can use to poll status instead of resubmitting. We'll add that to action items.
[06:34] Priya: about VPC: we run Redwood in our VPC with private subnets, and we control node images. We delayed driver updates, so some nodes are on 520.* drivers and others on 525.*. Could mixed drivers cause kernel mismatch?
[06:56] Samir: mixed driver versions across nodes shouldn't be an issue for single node work, but if pods move or a node drains and gets rescheduled, different drivers may expose different kernel behaviors. We recommend standardizing on supported driver versions - I'll share Redwood's tested matrix.
[07:15] Alex: noted - Samir to share driver/compat matrix.
[07:22] Jordan: what about memory pinning and cudaMallocManaged vs explicit cudaMalloc? we saw in the runtime some kernels use unified memory which spikes host memory too.
[07:39] Samir: yes we use a mix. unified memory can cause page faults and unexpected host-GPU transfers; for low-latency inference, we prefer explicit device allocations and pre-warm memory pools. In our production optimized kernels we pre-allocate the per-batch workspace to prevent fragmentation. If you have lots of concurrent sessions with variable seq lengths it can still fragment.
[08:05] Marco: how does KV cache factor in? we only store per-session key/vals on GPU - but when sessions hit 50k tokens total across turns it's huge.
[08:22] Samir: two levers: you can evict older prefixes (LRU policy) or compress the KV with quantization (fp16 vs int8) and chunk the cache to host memory when cold. both have tradeoffs in latency. For stringent latency SLOs, keep active KV on GPU and offload cold sessions to host or disk.
[08:45] Priya: the latency SLO is 300ms p95 for short queries, but heavy sessions can be 2-4s - that's tolerated. Problem is long requests cause node death affecting short queries.
[09:03] Maya: that implies isolation of heavy sessions. we can run dedicated pools for long-context work. Redwood supports routing rules to send >=X token requests to a different pool.
[09:19] Alex: we discussed earlier about admission control. we can enforce a per-request token limit at the gateway and return 413 style response or route to a slow-path pool.
[09:33] Priya: okay, would prefer routing to a larger memory pool rather than outright rejecting.
[09:40] Samir: fine - we should size those nodes with more HBM or GPUs with larger memory and disable aggressive batch coalescing on that pool. coalescing helps throughput but combines requests and can multiply memory use.
[09:58] Marco: what's the interaction between coalescing and retries? if multiple clients retry, coalescing may pack them and cause bigger allocations, right?
[10:13] Samir: exactly. coalescing is great for small, similar length requests, but in the presence of retry storms it can amplify. We recommend adaptive coalescing: lower coalesce window under high tail latencies and rate-limit client retries.
[10:30] Jordan: let's talk about timeouts - we saw some 5s timeouts at the LB and then client retried. what layers are timing out first?
[10:44] Maya: there are at least three: client SDK default (2-5s), LB (NGINX) idle timeout, and the agent-level execution timeout. If agent process blocks on GPU for long, the LB may timeout and the client retries.
[11:05] Samir: we can surface a short-running 'start-ack' header so clients see that work started, and then avoid retrying. Also agent-level pre-flight checks could reject if likely to exceed request timeout.
[11:21] Priya: I'd like to see suggested default timeouts and SDK best practices.
[11:27] Alex: we'll share recommended SDK config for Nimbus.
[11:30] Marco: one more thing: quantization differences - sometimes int8 reduces memory but raises chance of kernel fallback that is slower on some GPU architectures. did you observe slower kernels when quantizing?
[11:45] Samir: yes - quantized kernels can use different fused ops; on some older GPUs the optimized int8 kernels are slower than fp16. Kernel selection logic picks best path per model/sequence. we'll share model-specific perf numbers.
[12:02] Priya: is there a way to let us pin kernel selection so we can test a stable configuration?
[12:10] Samir: yes we support per-deployment kernel override. Useful for testbeds.
[12:16] Jordan: back to retries and charging - we got charged for repeated partial runs; how does Redwood handle billing when an execution started but crashed?
[12:27] Alex: billing is per-token and per-exec in our current model; partial executions are billed proportionally to tokens produced. We have a rollback policy for driver crashes if the runtime can detect crash before commit, but we need better telemetry to correlate client retries and double runs.
[12:45] Maya: can we get more granular logs? timestamps, request ids, gpu memory used per request?
[12:53] Samir: yes - action item: we'll collect GPU-level logs (nvidia-smi, driver logs), runtime traces, and provide a filtered timeline.
[13:05] Marco: also curious about preemption when we use spot instances. preemption sometimes kills nodes mid-exec and leaves partial credits.
[13:17] Samir: spot preemption is tricky. we recommend using reserved/dedicated for critical workflows, or use fast checkpoint/resume for tolerant workloads. we can also configure quick-fallback to hosted pools.
[13:30] Priya: about VPC specifics: we use internal KMS and an HSM for keys. does Redwood require outbound connections to validate key leases?
[13:41] Alex: for private deployments Redwood can run control plane in VPC; key wrapping can be performed locally. We'll document minimal egress.
[13:52] Jordan: ok, practically: what are the immediate mitigations we can apply while we wait for logs?
[14:00] Samir: short-term: 1) enable per-request token admission limit and route >X tokens to a large-pool, 2) lower coalesce window for your current pool, 3) set client SDK to retry=0 for non-idempotent generation calls and retry=1 for idempotent calls with exponential backoff, 4) standardize GPU driver across nodes.
[14:26] Priya: we'll try 1-3 today.
[14:30] Alex: great. next, we walked through actual log snippets you sent earlier (timestamps redacted) -
[14:40] Samir: (reads) "...allocation failed: out of memory while allocating 24,000,000 bytes... kernel aborted... cuda: driver rebooted..." - that's consistent with large activation allocations.
[15:00] Marco: we also saw vGPU memory fragmentation warnings.
[15:08] Samir: fragmentation can be caused by variable seq length and small ephemeral allocations; pre-warming a per-worker arena helps.
[15:24] Priya: what about the circuit breaker we discussed - stop accepting new sessions when node mem pressure > 85%?
[15:33] Maya: we've got metrics but thresholds aren't wired. we can add a mem-pressure circuit that moves session creation to other pools and triggers alerts.
[15:44] Samir: Redwood can expose a mem-pressure signal and we can implement an admission control webhook to reject or re-route.
[15:53] Jordan: can the runtime shed older sessions automatically?
[15:58] Samir: we have an optional background eviction policy: mark least-recently-used sessions for offload to host, but that adds IO latency when they come back. It's a tradeoff.
[16:12] Priya: OK. I'd like to run a staged stress test: the customer to provide workload, Redwood to run 2-hour bench on a mirrored VPC with driver matrix.
[16:24] Alex: agreed. We'll schedule bench, Samir will own log collection, Maya will help with autoscaler tweaks.
[16:34] Jordan: any security/compliance concerns about sharing logs? we need PII redaction.
[16:40] Maya: we'll scrub payloads - we'll only share performance traces and sanitized prompts.
[16:46] Samir: we'll also share the benchmark spreadsheet link and a suggested config for retry/backoff and coalescing.
[16:53] Alex: ok recap - (1) Samir share driver/compat matrix + kernel picks, (2) Nimbus provide workload, seq distributions, and sample prompts, (3) Redwood run 2-hour bench in mirror with different driver versions and quant settings, (4) agreed recommended SDK retry defaults and admission policy.
[17:15] Priya: sounds good. small nit - can you send an architecture diagram for the routing rules?
[17:22] Alex: yes I'll include a simple slide with routing rules and suggested pool sizes.
[17:28] Jordan: timeline? can we do bench next week?
[17:32] Samir: we can start bench as early as Thursday if Nimbus provides workload by Wednesday EOD.
[17:38] Alex: final Q on cost: what are expected unit cost changes if we move to larger memory GPUs for long-context pool?
[17:47] Samir: expect ~1.6-2x unit cost depending on perf; but intact throughput might be better for some workloads so cost per useful token may not double. We'll include cost estimate in the spreadsheet.
[17:58] Marco: thanks all.
[18:02] Alex: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the artifacts.
